meta.title: Accounting changes and error analysis
meta.summary: Types of accounting changes, retrospective application of changes in principle, impracticability and indirect effects, prospective changes in estimate including depreciation methods, corrections of errors as prior period adjustments, and counterbalancing and noncounterbalancing errors.

videos.title: Types of accounting changes
videos.take: Principle changes are retrospective; estimate changes are prospective; errors are restated

scenes.say: Bluestem has been public for three years. It's changing an inventory method, revising estimates, and it just found a mistake. Each is handled differently.

scenes.heading: Three types, three treatments
scenes.say: A change in accounting principle, like LIFO to FIFO, is applied retrospectively. A change in estimate, like a new useful life, is applied prospectively. Correcting an error restates prior statements through a prior period adjustment.
A fourth type, a change in reporting entity, such as presenting consolidated statements instead of individual ones, is also applied retrospectively.

Why the difference? Principle changes are restated so years are comparable on one method. Estimates aren't restated because they were the best information at the time. Errors are restated because the old statements were wrong.

sub: A new method for new events,
scenes.say: Adopting a method for transactions that are new or different in substance, or that were previously immaterial, isn't a change in principle.

scenes.q: Bluestem revises a machine's salvage value. This is:
scenes.say: Quick check. Bluestem revises a machine's salvage value. What kind of change is it? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, a change in estimate.

videos.title: Changes in principle: retrospective application
videos.take: Restate prior periods presented; adjust the opening retained earnings of the earliest period for earlier effects

scenes.say: Northwind Canoe used LIFO before Bluestem bought it. In 2031, Bluestem switches Northwind to FIFO to match the rest of the company.

sub: Apply the new principle as if it
scenes.say: Retrospective application means applying the new method to prior periods as if it had always been used. The change must be preferable, and justified in the notes.

scenes.heading: Pretax income, FIFO minus LIFO
scenes.say: FIFO would have given higher pretax income: $40,000 more in total before 2029, $20,000 more in 2029, and $30,000 more in 2030. The tax rate is twenty-five percent.

scenes.heading: Presenting 2031 with 2030 comparatives
scenes.say: Bluestem presents 2031 and 2030. It restates 2030 income upward by $22,500 after tax. Effects before 2030, $60,000 pretax or $45,000 after tax, adjust the January 1, 2030 retained earnings balance.

scenes.heading: Entry in 2031: cumulative to Jan 1, 2031
scenes.say: The 2031 entry records the full cumulative difference to January 1, 2031: $90,000 more inventory, $22,500 of deferred tax, and $67,500 to retained earnings.

scenes.q: A change in principle increases prior years' pretax income by $100,000 in total; tax rate 25%. Adjustment to beginning retained earnings?
scenes.say: Quick check. A change in principle increases prior years' pretax income by a hundred thousand in total; tax rate twenty-five percent. Adjustment to beginning retained earnings? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Direct effects, indirect effects and impracticability
videos.take: Restate direct effects only; if retrospective application is impracticable, apply from the earliest practicable date

scenes.say: Restating past years raises two practical questions.

scenes.heading: Direct vs indirect effects
scenes.say: Direct effects, like the change in inventory, cost of goods sold and taxes, are restated. Indirect effects, like employee bonuses that would have been higher under FIFO, aren't restated. They're recognized in the period of the change, if contractually owed.

Retrospective application is impracticable if, after every reasonable effort, the effects can't be determined: the records don't exist, management's past intent would have to be assumed, or estimates can't be objectively made.

Then the new principle is applied from the earliest date practicable, often prospectively. Changing to LIFO is the classic case: past LIFO layers usually can't be reconstructed, so the opening inventory becomes the first layer.

scenes.heading: Disclose
items: Nature of and reason for the change
Effects on each line and on EPS
scenes.say: The notes explain the nature of and reason for the change, why the new method is preferable, the effect on each line item and on EPS, and the cumulative effect on opening retained earnings.

scenes.q: Under a retrospective change, prior-year bonuses that depended on income are:
scenes.say: Quick check. Under a retrospective change, prior-year bonuses that depended on income are treated how? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, not restated: they're indirect effects.

videos.title: Changes in estimate
videos.take: Account for estimates prospectively; a change in depreciation method is a change in estimate effected by a change in principle

scenes.say: Bluestem's new thermoforming machine was depreciated double-declining-balance. After two years, the pattern of use looks steady, so it switches to straight-line.

scenes.big: Change in estimate effected by a change in principle
scenes.say: A change in depreciation method is a change in estimate effected by a change in accounting principle. It's inseparable from new information about how the asset's benefits are used, so it's accounted for prospectively.

scenes.heading: Thermoforming machine
scenes.say: The machine cost $400,000, with a five-year life and no salvage. Double-declining-balance took $160,000 and then $96,000, leaving a book value of $144,000. Straight-line over the remaining three years: $48,000 a year from now on.
No catch-up adjustment, no restatement. The remaining book value is simply spread over the remaining life using the new method.
The same prospective treatment applies to all estimates: credit losses, warranty costs, useful lives and salvage, obsolescence. Material changes are disclosed with their effect on income and EPS.

scenes.q: Book value $90,000 after 3 years; switch to straight-line; 6 years remain; salvage $6,000. New annual depreciation?
scenes.say: Quick check. Book value ninety thousand after three years; switch to straight-line; six years remain; salvage six thousand. New annual depreciation? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Correcting errors
videos.take: Correct prior-period errors as prior period adjustments to opening retained earnings, net of tax, and restate

scenes.say: During 2031, Sam discovers that 2030 depreciation of $50,000 on the Redwood Falls plant was never recorded.

scenes.heading: What counts as an error
scenes.say: Errors include mathematical mistakes, mistakes in applying GAAP, oversight or misuse of facts that existed when the statements were prepared, and changing from an unacceptable method to GAAP. Better information later isn't an error.

scenes.heading: The missed depreciation
scenes.say: 2030 depreciation was understated by $50,000, so 2030 income was overstated by $37,500 after tax.

scenes.heading: Prior period adjustment, 2031
scenes.say: Bluestem records a prior period adjustment: debit retained earnings for $37,500, adjust taxes for $12,500, and credit Accumulated Depreciation for $50,000. Nothing goes through 2031 income.

The 2030 comparative statements are restated, and the notes describe the error and its effects. A material error in issued statements is a restatement, often called a Big R, which damages credibility.

scenes.q: A prior-year expense of $80,000 was omitted; tax 25%. Prior period adjustment to retained earnings?
scenes.say: Quick check. A prior-year expense of eighty thousand was omitted; tax twenty-five percent. Prior period adjustment to retained earnings? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Counterbalancing and noncounterbalancing errors
videos.take: Counterbalancing errors correct themselves after two years; noncounterbalancing errors persist until fixed

scenes.say: Some errors fix themselves. Others never do.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of error
scenes.say: Counterbalancing errors, like a misstated ending inventory or a missed accrual, reverse themselves over two periods. Noncounterbalancing errors, like missed depreciation, don't.

scenes.heading: 2030 ending inventory understated $20,000
scenes.say: Suppose 2030's ending inventory was understated by $20,000. 2030 income was understated, 2031 income will be overstated, and by the end of 2031, retained earnings is correct.

scenes.heading: Found in 2031, books still open
scenes.say: If Bluestem finds the error in 2031 before closing the books, it corrects beginning inventory and retained earnings, net of tax. If the books for 2031 are already closed, no entry is needed, but the 2030 comparatives are still restated.
When several errors are found, analyze them year by year: the effect on each year's income, then on the balance sheet at each date. A worksheet helps keep the counterbalancing ones straight.

scenes.q: An accrued wage of $8,000 was missed at the end of 2030. If found after 2031's books are closed, the correcting entry is:
scenes.say: Quick check. An accrued wage of eight thousand was missed at the end of 2030. If it's found after 2031's books are closed, what's the correcting entry? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, none: it has counterbalanced. Comparatives are still restated.

case: Bluestem's 2031 audit finds: (1) 2030 depreciation of $50,000 omitted; (2) 2030 ending inventory understated $20,000; (3) the change of Northwind from LIFO to FIFO (cumulative pretax effect to January 1, 2031 of $90,000). Tax rate 25%. 2030 reported net income was $1,250,000. The founder wants to record everything in 2031 income 'to avoid a restatement'.
Compute the total adjustment to January 1, 2031 retained earnings.

Corrected 2030 NI: 1,250,000 − 37,500 + 15,000 + 22,500 (LIFO→FIFO 2030 effect) = 1,250,000. Items: (1) prior period adjustment; (2) prior period adjustment (counterbalances in 2031); (3) retrospective. Jan 1 2031 RE: −37,500 + 15,000 + 67,500 = +45,000. Recording in 2031 income violates GAAP and misstates trends; restatement and disclosure required.
